The central question is: when you extend a pretrained tokenizer with new vocabulary tokens to accommodate a domain-shifted corpus (e.g., adding biomedical or code-specific subwords), how do the resulting changes in subword fertility — the average number of tokens a word decomposes into — propagate into embedding space geometry and disrupt the continuity assumptions baked into the original pretraining? A beginner assumes tokenizer extension is a localized operation: new embeddings get initialized (often via averaging constituent subword embeddings), training proceeds, and the model adapts. What the expert sees instead is a dual fragmentation problem: the new tokens occupy embedding space positions that are geometrically inconsistent with the manifold structure learned during pretraining, while simultaneously the old tokens that previously covered domain-shifted terms now carry residual fertility load — they get called on less frequently and in altered co-occurrence contexts, destabilizing their embedding geometry without any explicit gradient signal targeting them. The subword fertility drift problem is particularly insidious because it is asymmetric: high-fertility decompositions of rare domain terms (e.g., "##yl" "##oxy" "##ben" "##zene" for benzene) get replaced by single tokens, collapsing what was a sequential composition of meaning into a point mass in embedding space with no pretraining history, while the constituent subwords that previously did that compositional work now have corrupted positional and co-occurrence statistics. The expert further worries about boundary misalignment at the sequence level: sentences that tokenize differently under the extended vocabulary produce different attention patterns, different positional encoding assignments, and different KV cache structures — meaning that even frozen layers upstream of any fine-tuning are processing structurally alien inputs relative to their calibration distribution.

Averaging constituent subword embeddings places the new token at the centroid of a simplex defined by its components, but the pretraining embedding manifold is not convex — it has anisotropic curvature, with high-frequency tokens clustering in dense, low-variance neighborhoods and rare tokens occupying sparse peripheral regions (Ethayarajh 2019 demonstrated that contextual embeddings occupy a narrow cone, meaning most of the ambient space is geometrically "dead"). The centroid initialization therefore almost certainly lands in a low-density void: it has the right direction approximately (cosine similarity to constituents is preserved) but the wrong magnitude and wrong local neighborhood density, violating the isotropy assumptions that attention dot-product scaling implicitly relies on — a token whose embedding norm is artificially compressed relative to its semantic neighbors will generate systematically suppressed attention logits. Early gradient descent worsens this because the loss signal the new token receives is dominated by its co-occurrence statistics in the new domain corpus, which are high-frequency and highly specific, so the optimizer pushes the embedding rapidly toward a region of embedding space tuned for domain fluency — but this region is far from where pretraining geometry would have placed a token of this semantic type, creating a discontinuity that neighboring old-token embeddings then have to adapt around. Karpukhin et al.'s DPR work and subsequent analysis of dense retrieval collapse showed that aggressive early-training updates to newly initialized embeddings can cause representation collapse in the surrounding neighborhood, pulling anchor embeddings off their pretrained positions. The DAPT (Domain-Adaptive Pretraining) work by Gururangan et al. (2020) sidestepped this partly by not extending the tokenizer, precisely because vocabulary extension destabilizes the embedding space in the early continual pretraining phase before the model can equilibrate. Quantitatively, Sachidananda et al. (2023) on vocabulary transfer found that the first ~1–5% of continual pretraining steps produce the highest embedding drift variance, confirming that gradient descent is maximally destructive to geometric coherence exactly when the new embeddings are most fragile.

response:
The feed-forward layers in late transformer blocks operate as associative memories where the first linear projection acts as a key lookup — a token's residual stream representation must land near a stored key vector to activate the corresponding value, and Geva et al. (2022) showed these keys correspond to human-interpretable semantic concepts clustered in specific embedding subspaces. When a new domain token's embedding drifts via gradient updates into a region previously occupied by semantically adjacent old tokens, it begins co-activating the same FF memory keys as those old tokens, but with a different residual stream context — this creates destructive interference in the value readout, analogous to aliasing in signal processing, where two distinct inputs now map to overlapping key activations and the superimposed value output is semantically incoherent for both. The old semantically adjacent tokens suffer what can be described as key eviction pressure: continued gradient updates that optimize the new token's FF memory access implicitly reshape the key subspace, and since FF weights are shared across all token positions, improving retrieval for the new token necessarily distorts retrieval for old tokens whose keys were geometrically nearby — Mitchell et al.'s ROME (2022) and MEMIT (2023) work on model editing demonstrated precisely this: editing one factual association corrupts semantically neighboring associations at rates proportional to their geometric proximity in the FF key space. Whether this constitutes a recoverable or permanent blind spot depends critically on training compute budget relative to the size of the affected neighborhood: if the domain corpus is large enough and training runs long enough, the model can in principle re-carve distinct key subspaces for old and new tokens through weight updates that increase their effective separation — but Scialom et al. (2022) on continual learning in LLMs found that without explicit regularization (e.g., EWC-style constraints on FF weights), semantically adjacent old-token retrieval degrades monotonically and does not self-correct even after 100B tokens of continued training. The blind spot is therefore semi-permanent under standard continual pretraining: the model retains the syntactic behavior of old adjacent tokens (handled in early layers that are less disrupted) but loses fine-grained semantic distinctions that depend on late-layer FF memory, producing a model that uses old tokens grammatically correctly but with subtly flattened or blended semantics — a failure mode that standard perplexity metrics on the new domain corpus will not detect because perplexity measures next-token prediction accuracy, not semantic precision of old-vocabulary retrieval.

response:
The most sensitive existing methodology is layer-wise probing with frozen classifiers trained on pretraining-era representations: you freeze a probe on the original model's late-layer activations for semantically adjacent old tokens, then measure probe accuracy degradation on the continually pretrained model — a drop in probe accuracy with no corresponding drop in generation fluency is the diagnostic signature of semantic flattening, and Conneau et al.'s SentEval suite and Tenney et al.'s edge probing benchmarks (2019) provide the infrastructure, though neither was designed specifically for this failure mode. A more targeted protocol is the semantic neighborhood consistency test: construct minimal pairs where an old adjacent token and the new domain token should produce divergent downstream predictions (e.g., "the compound was aromatic" vs. "the compound was benzene" in a property-prediction cloze task), and measure whether the model's internal representations for the old token have drifted toward the new token's representation using centered kernel alignment (CKA) — Kornblith et al. (2019) showed CKA is sensitive to representational similarity shifts that cosine similarity misses because it accounts for the full activation distribution rather than individual vector angles. The GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks are largely insensitive to this failure mode because their tasks are dominated by syntactic and surface coreference signals that survive semantic flattening intact; BioASQ and USMLE-style medical QA benchmarks are somewhat better because they require fine-grained semantic distinctions among near-synonymous domain terms, but even these conflate retrieval precision with domain knowledge acquisition. The sharpest existing tool is the knowledge neurons probing protocol from Dai et al. (2022), which identifies specific FF neuron activations responsible for factual associations and can detect when a neuron's activation pattern for an old token has been contaminated by new token gradient updates — this directly operationalizes the blind spot hypothesis as a measurable neuron-level interference metric. Practically, the field lacks a dedicated benchmark for this specific failure mode, and the closest approximation requires constructing synthetic evaluation sets where ground-truth semantic neighborhoods are known from the pretraining corpus statistics, then measuring post-continual-pretraining divergence in those neighborhoods using both probing accuracy and token substitution sensitivity — a methodology proposed but not yet standardized in the vocabulary transfer literature.
